text: Let $f:𝐑\to 𝐑$ be defined as $f(x)=\frac{2x^{2}-3x+2}{3x^{2}+x+3}$. Then $f$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To determine the nature of the given function, let us carefully analyze it for both the one-one (injective) and onto (surjective) properties. The function is given by:

$f(x)=\frac{2x^{2}-3x+2}{3x^{2}+x+3}$

where the domain is the set of real numbers $𝐑$ and the codomain is also $𝐑$.

Checking if the function is one-one

A function $f:𝐑\to 𝐑$ is said to be one-one if every element in the domain has a distinct image in the codomain. That is, if $f(x_{1})=f(x_{2})$, then we must have $x_{1}=x_{2}$.

Let us check if we can find two different real values of $x$ that give the same value for $f(x)$. Let us set $f(x)=1$ and solve for $x$:

$\frac{2x^{2}-3x+2}{3x^{2}+x+3}=1$

Cross-multiplying, we obtain:

$2x^{2}-3x+2=3x^{2}+x+3$

Bringing all terms to one side, we get:

$x^{2}+4x+1=0$

Using the quadratic formula to find the roots:

$x=\frac{-4\pm \sqrt{16-4(1)(1)}}{2}=\frac{-4\pm \sqrt{12}}{2}=-2\pm \sqrt{3}$

Since we found two distinct real values, $x_{1}=-2+\sqrt{3}$ and $x_{2}=-2-\sqrt{3}$, such that $f(x_{1})=f(x_{2})=1$, the function is not one-one.

Checking if the function is onto

A function is onto if its range is equal to its codomain. Here, the codomain is $𝐑$. To find the range, let us set $f(x)=y$:

$y=\frac{2x^{2}-3x+2}{3x^{2}+x+3}$

Cross-multiplying gives us:

$y(3x^{2}+x+3)=2x^{2}-3x+2$

$3yx^{2}+yx+3y=2x^{2}-3x+2$

Grouping the terms by the powers of $x$, we form a quadratic equation in $x$:

$(3y-2)x^{2}+(y+3)x+(3y-2)=0$

Since $x$ is a real number, the discriminant ($D$) of this quadratic equation must be greater than or equal to zero ($D\geq 0$).

$D=(y+3)^{2}-4(3y-2)(3y-2)\geq 0$

$(y+3)^{2}-4(3y-2)^{2}\geq 0$

This is in the form of $a^{2}-b^{2}\geq 0$, which can be factored as $(a-b)(a+b)\geq 0$. Here, $a=y+3$ and $b=2(3y-2)=6y-4$:

$[(y+3)-(6y-4)][(y+3)+(6y-4)]\geq 0$

$(-5y+7)(7y-1)\geq 0$

To solve this inequality, we can multiply by $-1$ (which reverses the inequality sign):

$(5y-7)(7y-1)\leq 0$

The critical points are $y=\frac{1}{7}$ and $y=\frac{7}{5}$. Based on the inequality, $y$ must lie between these two values:

$\frac{1}{7}\leq y\leq \frac{7}{5}$

This means the range of the function is the closed interval $\left [\frac{1}{7},\frac{7}{5}\right ]$. 

Because the range is a small subset of the real numbers and not equal to the entire codomain $𝐑$, the function is not onto.

Conclusion:

Since $f(x)$ is neither one-one nor onto, the correct statement is given by Option D.

Option D

text: Consider the quadratic equation $\left (n^{2}-2n+2\right )x^{2}-3x+\left (n^{2}-2n+2\right )^{2}=0,n\in 𝐑$. Let $α$ be the minimum value of the product of its roots and $β$ be the maximum value of the sum of its roots. Then the sum of the first six terms of the G.P., whose first term is $α$ and the common ratio is $\frac{α}{β}$, is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For the quadratic equation

$\left (n^{2}-2n+2\right )x^{2}-3x+\left (n^{2}-2n+2\right )^{2}=0,$

let us first compare it with the standard quadratic form

$ax^{2}+bx+c=0.$

So,

$a=n^{2}-2n+2,b=-3,c=\left (n^{2}-2n+2\right )^{2}.$

Now rewrite $a$ in a simpler form:

$n^{2}-2n+2=(n-1)^{2}+1.$

Hence,

$a=(n-1)^{2}+1.$

Since $(n-1)^{2}\geq 0$, we get

$a\geq 1.$

Now, for a quadratic equation, by Vieta’s formulas:

Sum of roots $=-\dfrac{b}{a}$

Product of roots $=\dfrac{c}{a}$

So here,

$\text{Sum of roots}=\frac{3}{a}$

and

$\text{Product of roots}=\frac{a^{2}}{a}=a.$

Therefore,

$\text{Product of roots}=(n-1)^{2}+1.$

So the minimum value of the product is clearly

$α=1,$

attained when $n=1$.

Now the sum of roots is

$\frac{3}{(n-1)^{2}+1}.$

Since the denominator is minimum when $(n-1)^{2}=0$, the maximum value of the sum is

$β=\frac{3}{1}=3.$

So we have

$α=1,β=3.$

Now the G.P. has

first term $a=α=1$

common ratio $r=\dfrac{α}{β}=\dfrac{1}{3}$

We need the sum of first six terms:

$S_{6}=a\cdot \frac{1-r^{6}}{1-r}.$

Substitute the values:

$S_{6}=1\cdot \frac{1-\left (\frac{1}{3}\right )^{6}}{1-\frac{1}{3}}.$

Now,

$\left (\frac{1}{3}\right )^{6}=\frac{1}{729}$

and

$1-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}.$

Hence,

$S_{6}=\frac{1-\frac{1}{729}}{\frac{2}{3}}=\frac{\frac{728}{729}}{\frac{2}{3}}=\frac{728}{729}\cdot \frac{3}{2}.$

So,

$S_{6}=\frac{1092}{729}=\frac{364}{243}.$

Therefore, the required sum is

$\dfrac{364}{243}.$

So the correct option is

$\text{Option C}.$

text: A building has ground floor and 10 more floors. Nine persons enter in a lift at the ground floor. The lift goes up to the $10^{\text{th}}$ floor. The number of ways, in which any 4 persons exit at a floor and the remaining 5 persons exit at a different floor, if the lift does not stop at the first and the second floors, is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
First, decide which $4$ out of the $9$ persons will get down together. The remaining $5$ persons are then fixed automatically.

Number of ways to form the two groups of sizes $4$ and $5$ is $\frac{9!}{4!5!}=126$

Now, the lift does not stop at the $1^{\text{st}}$ and $2^{\text{nd}}$ floors. So people can get down only on floors $3$ to $10$, i.e., $8$ possible floors.

Choose any $2$ different floors out of these $8$ floors for the two groups to exit: ${}^{8}\mathrm{C}_{2}=28$

After choosing the two floors, we must decide which floor is for the group of $4$ and which floor is for the group of $5$. This can be done in $2$ ways.

So, total number of ways is $126\times 28\times 2=7056$

text: Let the mean and the variance of seven observations $2,4,α,8,β,12,14,α<β$, be 8 and 16 respectively. Then the quadratic equation whose roots are $3α+2$ and $2β+1$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To find the required quadratic equation, we must first find the values of $α$ and $β$. 

Given that there are 7 observations: $2,4,α,8,β,12,14$. Let $n=7$.

The mean of these observations ($\bar{x}$) is $8$. 

According to the formula for the mean:

$\bar{x}=\frac{\sum x_{i}}{n}$

Substituting the given values:

$8=\frac{2+4+α+8+β+12+14}{7}$

$56=40+α+β$

$α+β=16\text{--- (1)}$

Next, the variance ($σ^{2}$) is given as $16$. The formula for variance is:

$σ^{2}=\frac{\sum x_{i}^{2}}{n}-(\bar{x})^{2}$

Substituting the known values:

$16=\frac{2^{2}+4^{2}+α^{2}+8^{2}+β^{2}+12^{2}+14^{2}}{7}-(8)^{2}$

$16=\frac{4+16+α^{2}+64+β^{2}+144+196}{7}-64$

$16+64=\frac{424+α^{2}+β^{2}}{7}$

$80\times 7=424+α^{2}+β^{2}$

$560=424+α^{2}+β^{2}$

$α^{2}+β^{2}=136\text{--- (2)}$

Now, using the algebraic identity $(α+β)^{2}=α^{2}+β^{2}+2αβ$, we can find the product $αβ$:

$(16)^{2}=136+2αβ$

$256=136+2αβ$

$2αβ=120$

$αβ=60$

The numbers $α$ and $β$ are the roots of the quadratic equation $t^{2}-(α+β)t+αβ=0$:

$t^{2}-16t+60=0$

$t^{2}-10t-6t+60=0$

$t(t-10)-6(t-10)=0$

$(t-6)(t-10)=0$

Thus, the values are $6$ and $10$. Since we are given that $α<β$, we have:

$α=6$

$β=10$

We are asked to find the quadratic equation whose roots are $3α+2$ and $2β+1$. Let's evaluate these roots:

$\text{First root}=3(6)+2=18+2=20$

$\text{Second root}=2(10)+1=20+1=21$

Now, let's find the sum and the product of the roots for our new quadratic equation:

$\text{Sum of roots}=20+21=41$

$\text{Product of roots}=20\times 21=420$

The standard form of a quadratic equation is $x^{2}-(\text{Sum of roots})x+(\text{Product of roots})=0$.

Substituting the values:

$x^{2}-41x+420=0$

Hence, the correct option is Option B.

text: A bag contains 6 blue and 6 green balls. Pairs of balls are drawn without replacement until the bag is empty. The probability that each drawn pair consists of one blue and one green ball is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Drawing pairs until the bag is empty splits the 12 balls into 6 pairs; the order in which the pairs come out multiplies the favourable and total counts by the same factor $6!$, so only the split into pairs matters, and all splits are equally likely.

Number of ways to split 12 distinct balls into 6 unordered pairs:

$\dfrac{12!}{(2!)^{6}\qquad 6!}=10395$

In a favourable split each blue ball is paired with a different green ball, so the 6 blue balls are matched with the 6 green balls in $6!=720$ ways.

$P=\dfrac{720}{10395}=\dfrac{16}{231}$

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text: Let C be a circle having centre in the first quadrant and touching the $x$-axis at a distance of 3 units from the origin. If the circle $C$ has an intercept of length $6\sqrt{3}$ on $y$-axis, then the length of the chord of the circle C on the line $x-y=3$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Since the circle touches the $x$-axis at a point which is $3$ units from the origin, the point of contact is $(3,0)$.

The centre lies in the first quadrant and the radius is perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact. So, the centre must be of the form $(3,r)$, where $r$ is the radius.

The circle has an intercept of length $6\sqrt{3}$ on the $y$-axis. This means the chord cut by the line $x=0$ has length $6\sqrt{3}$.

For a circle of radius $r$, if the distance of a chord from the centre is $d$, then chord length is $2\sqrt{r^{2}-d^{2}}$.

Here, the distance from centre $(3,r)$ to the $y$-axis $(x=0)$ is $d=3$. So the intercept on the $y$-axis is

$2\sqrt{r^{2}-3^{2}}=6\sqrt{3}$

So,

$\sqrt{r^{2}-9}=3\sqrt{3}\Rightarrow r^{2}-9=27\Rightarrow r^{2}=36\Rightarrow r=6$

Hence, centre of the circle is $(3,6)$ and radius is $6$ units.


[IMG]


Now we need the length of the chord cut by the line $x-y=3$.

First find the perpendicular distance $p$ from the centre $(3,6)$ to the line $x-y-3=0$:

$p=\frac{|1\cdot 3+(-1)\cdot 6-3|}{\sqrt{1^{2}+(-1)^{2}}}=\frac{|3-6-3|}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}}$

Now chord length on this line is

$PQ=2\sqrt{6^{2}-p^{2}}\therefore p=\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}}$

$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{p}=\dfrac{|3-6-3|}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \mathrm{PQ}=2\sqrt{36-\dfrac{36}{2}} \\ =2\times \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{2}}=6\sqrt{2} \end{array}$

text: The eccentricity of an ellipse $E$ with centre at the origin $O$ is $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and its directrices are $x=\pm \frac{4\sqrt{6}}{3}$. Let $\mathrm{H}:\frac{x^{2}}{\mathrm{a}^{2}}-\frac{y^{2}}{\mathrm{b}^{2}}=1$ be a hyperbola whose eccentricity is equal to the length of semi-major axis of E , and whose length of latus rectum is equal to the length of minor axis of E . Then the distance between the foci of H is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For the ellipse $E$, let its equation be

$\frac{x^{2}}{A^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{B^{2}}=1,A>B$

since its major axis is along the $x$-axis because the directrices are of the form $x=\text{constant}$.

Given eccentricity,

$e=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

For an ellipse with major axis along the $x$-axis, the directrices are

$x=\pm \frac{A}{e}$

We are given

$x=\pm \frac{4\sqrt{6}}{3}$

So,

$\frac{A}{e}=\frac{4\sqrt{6}}{3}$

Substituting $e=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$,

$A=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot \frac{4\sqrt{6}}{3}$

$A=\frac{4\sqrt{18}}{6}=\frac{4\cdot 3\sqrt{2}}{6}=2\sqrt{2}$

Thus the semi-major axis of ellipse $E$ is

$A=2\sqrt{2}$

Now for the ellipse,

$B^{2}=A^{2}(1-e^{2})$

Since

$A^{2}=(2\sqrt{2})^{2}=8$

and

$e^{2}=\frac{3}{4}$

we get

$B^{2}=8\left (1-\frac{3}{4}\right )=8\cdot \frac{1}{4}=2$

Hence

$B=\sqrt{2}$

So the length of minor axis of $E$ is

$2B=2\sqrt{2}$

Now consider the hyperbola

$H:\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}-\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$

Its eccentricity is equal to the length of semi-major axis of $E$, so

$e_{H}=2\sqrt{2}$

For a hyperbola,

$e_{H}^{2}=1+\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}$

Thus,

$(2\sqrt{2})^{2}=1+\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}$

$8=1+\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}$

$\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}=7\Rightarrow b^{2}=7a^{2}$

Also, the length of latus rectum of the hyperbola is equal to the length of minor axis of $E$.

For the hyperbola, length of latus rectum is

$\frac{2b^{2}}{a}$

So,

$\frac{2b^{2}}{a}=2\sqrt{2}$

$\frac{b^{2}}{a}=\sqrt{2}$

Using $b^{2}=7a^{2}$,

$\frac{7a^{2}}{a}=\sqrt{2}$

$7a=\sqrt{2}$

$a=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{7}$

Now for the hyperbola,

$c=ae_{H}$

So,

$c=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{7}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}=\frac{4}{7}$

Distance between the foci $=2c$,

$2c=\frac{8}{7}$

Hence, the correct answer is

$\dfrac{8}{7}$

So, Option D is correct.

text: Let $x=9$ be a directrix of an ellipse E , whose centre is at the origin and eccentricity is $\frac{1}{3}$. Let $\mathrm{P}(α,0)$, $α>0$, be a focus of E and AB be a chord passing through P . Then the locus of the mid point of AB is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Since the centre of the ellipse is at the origin and one directrix is $x=9$, the major axis is along the $x$-axis.

Let the ellipse be

$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$

with eccentricity

$e=\frac{1}{3}$

For an ellipse with major axis along the $x$-axis, the directrices are

$x=\pm \frac{a}{e}$

Given one directrix is $x=9$, so

$\frac{a}{e}=9$

Since $e=\frac{1}{3}$,

$a=9\cdot \frac{1}{3}=3$

Also,

$c=ae=3\cdot \frac{1}{3}=1$

So the focus $P(α,0)$ is

$P=(1,0)$

Hence $α=1$.

Now,

$b^{2}=a^{2}(1-e^{2})=9\left (1-\frac{1}{9}\right )=9\cdot \frac{8}{9}=8$

Therefore the ellipse is

$\frac{x^{2}}{9}+\frac{y^{2}}{8}=1$

Let the midpoint of chord $AB$ passing through the focus $(1,0)$ be $(h,k)$.

For the ellipse

$\frac{x^{2}}{9}+\frac{y^{2}}{8}=1$

the equation of the chord whose midpoint is $(h,k)$ is given by the NCERT midpoint formula:

$\frac{xx_{1}}{9}+\frac{yy_{1}}{8}=\frac{x_{1}^{2}}{9}+\frac{y_{1}^{2}}{8}$

So here the chord with midpoint $(h,k)$ is

$\frac{xh}{9}+\frac{yk}{8}=\frac{h^{2}}{9}+\frac{k^{2}}{8}$

Since this chord passes through the focus $(1,0)$, substitute $(x,y)=(1,0)$:

$\frac{h}{9}=\frac{h^{2}}{9}+\frac{k^{2}}{8}$

Multiply by $72$:

$8h=8h^{2}+9k^{2}$

So,

$9k^{2}=8h-8h^{2}=8h(1-h)$

Replacing $(h,k)$ by $(x,y)$ for the locus of the midpoint, we get

$9y^{2}=8x(1-x)$

Hence the required locus is

$9y^{2}=8x(1-x)$

So the correct option is A.

text: If $\sin \left (\tan ^{-1}(x\sqrt{2})\right )=\cot \left (\sin ^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\right ),x\in (0,1)$, then the value of $x$ is:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For $x\in (0,1)$, let $θ=\tan ^{-1}(x\sqrt{2})$, an acute angle with $\tan θ=x\sqrt{2}$, so

$\sin \left (\tan ^{-1}(x\sqrt{2})\right )=\frac{x\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{1+2x^{2}}}$

Let $𝜙=\sin ^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$, an acute angle with $\sin 𝜙=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$ and $\cos 𝜙=\sqrt{1-(1-x^{2})}=x$, so

$\cot \left (\sin ^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\right )=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$

Equating the two and cancelling $x\neq 0$:

$\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{1+2x^{2}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\Rightarrow 2(1-x^{2})=1+2x^{2}\Rightarrow x^{2}=\frac{1}{4}$

Since $x\in (0,1)$, $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

text: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-4}{1}=\frac{y-3}{2}=\frac{z-2}{-3}$ and $\frac{x+2}{2}=\frac{y-6}{4}=\frac{z-5}{-5}$ is:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For the two lines

$\frac{x-4}{1}=\frac{y-3}{2}=\frac{z-2}{-3}$

and

$\frac{x+2}{2}=\frac{y-6}{4}=\frac{z-5}{-5},$

we use the NCERT formula for the shortest distance between two skew lines:

$\text{Shortest distance}=\frac{\left |(⃗{a_{2}}-⃗{a_{1}})\cdot (⃗{b_{1}}\times ⃗{b_{2}})\right |}{\left |⃗{b_{1}}\times ⃗{b_{2}}\right |}$

where:

$⃗{a_{1}}$ is a point on the first line

$⃗{a_{2}}$ is a point on the second line

$⃗{b_{1}},⃗{b_{2}}$ are direction vectors of the two lines

Step 1: Identify points and direction vectors

From the first line,

$\frac{x-4}{1}=\frac{y-3}{2}=\frac{z-2}{-3}$

a point on it is

$A(4,3,2)$

and its direction vector is

$⃗{b_{1}}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$

From the second line,

$\frac{x+2}{2}=\frac{y-6}{4}=\frac{z-5}{-5}$

a point on it is

$B(-2,6,5)$

and its direction vector is

$⃗{b_{2}}=2\hat{i}+4\hat{j}-5\hat{k}$

Step 2: Find $⃗{AB}$

$⃗{AB}=B-A=(-2-4,6-3,5-2)=(-6,3,3)$

So,

$⃗{AB}=-6\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$

Step 3: Find $⃗{b_{1}}\times ⃗{b_{2}}$

$⃗{b_{1}}\times ⃗{b_{2}}=\left |\begin{array}{lll} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & 4 & -5 \end{array}\right |$

Expanding,

$=\hat{i}(2(-5)-(-3)(4))-\hat{j}(1(-5)-(-3)(2))+\hat{k}(1\cdot 4-2\cdot 2)$

$=\hat{i}(-10+12)-\hat{j}(-5+6)+\hat{k}(4-4)$

$=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+0\hat{k}$

So,

$⃗{b_{1}}\times ⃗{b_{2}}=(2,-1,0)$

Its magnitude is

$\left |⃗{b_{1}}\times ⃗{b_{2}}\right |=\sqrt{2^{2}+(-1)^{2}+0^{2}}=\sqrt{5}$

Step 4: Find scalar triple product

$⃗{AB}\cdot (⃗{b_{1}}\times ⃗{b_{2}})=(-6,3,3)\cdot (2,-1,0)$

$=(-6)(2)+(3)(-1)+(3)(0)$

$=-12-3=-15$

So,

$\left |⃗{AB}\cdot (⃗{b_{1}}\times ⃗{b_{2}})\right |=15$

Step 5: Find shortest distance

$d=\frac{15}{\sqrt{5}}=3\sqrt{5}$

Hence, the shortest distance is

$3\sqrt{5}$

So, the correct option is:

$\text{Option C}$

text: Let $\vec{\mathrm{a}}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{\mathrm{b}}=6\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$. Then the square of the area of the triangle with adjacent sides determined by the vectors $(2⃗{a}+3⃗{b})$ and $(⃗{a}-⃗{b})$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given

$⃗{a}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k},⃗{b}=6\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$

We need the square of the area of the triangle whose adjacent sides are

$2⃗{a}+3⃗{b}\text{and}⃗{a}-⃗{b}$

For two adjacent sides $⃗{u}$ and $⃗{v}$, area of triangle is

$\frac{1}{2}|⃗{u}\times ⃗{v}|$

So, square of the area is

$\left (\frac{1}{2}|⃗{u}\times ⃗{v}|\right )^{2}=\frac{1}{4}|⃗{u}\times ⃗{v}|^{2}$

Let

$⃗{u}=2⃗{a}+3⃗{b},⃗{v}=⃗{a}-⃗{b}$

First find $⃗{u}$:

$2⃗{a}=2(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k})=4\hat{i}+6\hat{j}+6\hat{k}$

$3⃗{b}=3(6\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k})=18\hat{i}+9\hat{j}+9\hat{k}$

Therefore,

$⃗{u}=2⃗{a}+3⃗{b}=22\hat{i}+15\hat{j}+15\hat{k}$

Now find $⃗{v}$:

$⃗{v}=⃗{a}-⃗{b}=(2-6)\hat{i}+(3-3)\hat{j}+(3-3)\hat{k}=-4\hat{i}$

Now compute $⃗{u}\times ⃗{v}$:

$⃗{u}\times ⃗{v}=\left |\begin{array}{lll} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 22 & 15 & 15 \\ -4 & 0 & 0 \end{array}\right |$

Expanding,

$⃗{u}\times ⃗{v}=\hat{i}(15\cdot 0-15\cdot 0)-\hat{j}(22\cdot 0-15\cdot (-4))+\hat{k}(22\cdot 0-15\cdot (-4))$

$=0\hat{i}-60\hat{j}+60\hat{k}$

So,

$|⃗{u}\times ⃗{v}|^{2}=0^{2}+(-60)^{2}+60^{2}=3600+3600=7200$

Hence square of the area of the triangle is

$\frac{1}{4}\times 7200=1800$

Therefore, the correct answer is

$1800$

So, Option C is correct.

text: Let $\lim _{x\to 2}\frac{(\tan (x-2))\left (\mathrm{r}x^{2}+(\mathrm{p}-2)x-2\mathrm{p}\right )}{(x-2)^{2}}=5$ for some $\mathrm{r},\mathrm{p}\in 𝑹$. If the set of all possible values of q , such that the roots of the equation $\mathrm{r}x^{2}-\mathrm{p}x+\mathrm{q}=0$ lie in $(0,2)$, be the interval $(α,β]$, then $4(α+β)$ equals :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
We are given

$\lim _{x\to 2}\frac{\tan (x-2)\left (rx^{2}+(p-2)x-2p\right )}{(x-2)^{2}}=5.$

We have to first find the relation between $r$ and $p$, and then determine all values of $q$ for which the roots of

$rx^{2}-px+q=0$

lie in $(0,2)$.

Step 1: Simplify the limit
Let

$f(x)=rx^{2}+(p-2)x-2p.$

Then the given limit becomes

$\lim _{x\to 2}\frac{\tan (x-2)f(x)}{(x-2)^{2}}=5.$

Now, as $x\to 2$,

$\tan (x-2)\sim x-2.$

So the limit becomes

$\lim _{x\to 2}\frac{(x-2)f(x)}{(x-2)^{2}}=\lim _{x\to 2}\frac{f(x)}{x-2}.$

For this limit to be finite, we must have

$f(2)=0.$

Now,

$f(2)=r(2)^{2}+(p-2)(2)-2p=4r+2p-4-2p=4r-4.$

So,

$4r-4=0⟹r=1.$

Then

$f(x)=x^{2}+(p-2)x-2p.$

Since $f(2)=0$, factor $(x-2)$:

$x^{2}+(p-2)x-2p=(x-2)(x+p).$

Hence the limit becomes

$\lim _{x\to 2}\frac{\tan (x-2)(x-2)(x+p)}{(x-2)^{2}}=\lim _{x\to 2}\frac{\tan (x-2)}{x-2}(x+p).$

Using

$\lim _{t\to 0}\frac{\tan t}{t}=1,$

we get

$1\cdot (2+p)=5.$

So,

$p+2=5⟹p=3.$

Thus,

$r=1,p=3.$

Step 2: Form the quadratic equation
Now the equation becomes

$x^{2}-3x+q=0.$

We want both roots to lie in $(0,2)$.

Let the roots be $α_{1},α_{2}$. Then

$α_{1}+α_{2}=3,α_{1}α_{2}=q.$

Since both roots lie in $(0,2)$, let us find the condition on $q$.

Step 3: Use condition for both roots in $(0,2)$
Let

$f(x)=x^{2}-3x+q.$

Since coefficient of $x^{2}$ is positive, parabola opens upward.

For both roots to lie in $(0,2)$, we need:

1. Real roots
So discriminant must be non-negative:

$\Delta =9-4q\geq 0⟹q\leq \frac{9}{4}.$

2. Both roots positive
Since product of roots is $q$,

$q>0.$

3. Both roots less than $2$
Now check value at $x=2$:

$f(2)=4-6+q=q-2.$

If both roots are less than $2$, then for an upward parabola, point $x=2$ lies to the right of both roots, so we need

$f(2)>0.$

Thus,

$q-2>0⟹q>2.$

Now combine:

$2<q\leq \frac{9}{4}.$

So the set of all possible values of $q$ is

$(α,β]=(2,\frac{9}{4}].$

Hence,

$α=2,β=\frac{9}{4}.$

Therefore,

$4(α+β)=4\left (2+\frac{9}{4}\right )=4\left (\frac{17}{4}\right )=17.$

Final Answer
$17$

So, the correct option is Option C.

text: Let $\mathrm{A}=\left [\begin{array}{lll} 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & α \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \end{array}\right ]$ be a singular matrix. Let $f(x)=\int\limits _{0}^{x}\left (\mathrm{t}^{2}+2\mathrm{t}+3\right )\mathrm{dt},x\in [1,α]$. If M and m are respectively the maximum and the minimum values of $f$ in $[1,α]$, then $3(\mathrm{M}-\mathrm{m})$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Since $A$ is a singular matrix, its determinant must be zero.

We have

$A=\left [\begin{array}{lll} 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & α \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \end{array}\right ]$

So,

$|A|=0$

Now let us calculate the determinant by expanding along the first row:

$|A|=1\left |\begin{array}{ll} 1 & α \\ 1 & -1 \end{array}\right |-3\left |\begin{array}{ll} 2 & α \\ 0 & -1 \end{array}\right |+(-1)\left |\begin{array}{ll} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array}\right |$

$=1[(1)(-1)-(α)(1)]-3[(2)(-1)-(α)(0)]-1[(2)(1)-(1)(0)]$

$=(-1-α)-3(-2)-2$

$=-1-α+6-2$

$=3-α$

Since $|A|=0$,

$3-α=0\Rightarrow α=3$

Now,

$f(x)=\int\limits _{0}^{x}(t^{2}+2t+3)dt$

Integrating,

$f(x)=\left [\frac{t^{3}}{3}+t^{2}+3t\right ]_{0}^{x}=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x^{2}+3x$

We need maximum and minimum values of $f(x)$ in $[1,α]=[1,3]$.

Now check whether $f(x)$ is increasing or decreasing.

$f^{'}(x)=x^{2}+2x+3$

$f^{'}(x)=x^{2}+2x+3=(x+1)^{2}+2>0\text{for all}x$

So $f(x)$ is strictly increasing on $[1,3]$.

Hence,

minimum value at $x=1$

maximum value at $x=3$

Now,

$m=f(1)=\frac{1}{3}+1+3=\frac{13}{3}$

and

$M=f(3)=\frac{27}{3}+9+9=9+9+9=27$

Therefore,

$M-m=27-\frac{13}{3}=\frac{81-13}{3}=\frac{68}{3}$

So,

$3(M-m)=3\cdot \frac{68}{3}=68$

Hence the correct answer is:

$68$

So, the correct option is $\text{Option B}$.

text:
Let $f:𝐑\to 𝐑$ be such that $f(xy)=f(x)f(y)$, for all $x,y\in 𝐑$ and $f(0)\neq 0$. Let $g:[1,\infty )\to 𝐑$ be a differentiable function such that

$x^{2}g(x)=\int\limits _{1}^{x}\left (\mathrm{t}^{2}f(\mathrm{t})-\mathrm{tg}(\mathrm{t})\right )dt$

Then $g(2)$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
We are given

$f(xy)=f(x)f(y)\text{for all}x,y\in \mathrm{ℝ},$

and

$f(0)\neq 0.$

Also,

$x^{2}g(x)=\int\limits _{1}^{x}\left (t^{2}f(t)-tg(t)\right )dt,x\geq 1.$

We have to find $g(2)$.

Step 1: Use the condition on $f$
Given

$f(xy)=f(x)f(y)$

for all real $x,y$.

Now put $x=0$ and any real $y$. Then

$f(0\cdot y)=f(0)f(y)$

that is,

$f(0)=f(0)f(y).$

Since $f(0)\neq 0$, we can divide by $f(0)$:

$f(y)=1\text{for all}y\in \mathrm{ℝ}.$

So,

$f(t)=1\text{for all}t.$

Step 2: Substitute into the given integral equation
The equation becomes

$x^{2}g(x)=\int\limits _{1}^{x}(t^{2}-tg(t))dt.$

Step 3: Differentiate both sides
Differentiate with respect to $x$.

Left side:

$\frac{d}{dx}[x^{2}g(x)]=x^{2}g^{'}(x)+2xg(x).$

Right side, by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus:

$\frac{d}{dx}\int\limits _{1}^{x}(t^{2}-tg(t))dt=x^{2}-xg(x).$

Hence,

$x^{2}g^{'}(x)+2xg(x)=x^{2}-xg(x).$

So,

$x^{2}g^{'}(x)+3xg(x)=x^{2}.$

Divide by $x$ (since $x\geq 1$):

$xg^{'}(x)+3g(x)=x.$

Or,

$g^{'}(x)+\frac{3}{x}g(x)=1.$

Step 4: Solve the differential equation
This is a linear differential equation:

$g^{'}(x)+\frac{3}{x}g(x)=1.$

Its integrating factor is

$\mathrm{I}.\mathrm{F}.=e^{\int \frac{3}{x}dx}=e^{3\ln x}=x^{3}.$

Multiply both sides by $x^{3}$:

$x^{3}g^{'}(x)+3x^{2}g(x)=x^{3}.$

The left side is

$\frac{d}{dx}(x^{3}g(x)).$

So,

$\frac{d}{dx}(x^{3}g(x))=x^{3}.$

Integrate:

$x^{3}g(x)=\frac{x^{4}}{4}+C.$

Thus,

$g(x)=\frac{x}{4}+\frac{C}{x^{3}}.$

Step 5: Find the constant using the original equation
Put $x=1$ in

$x^{2}g(x)=\int\limits _{1}^{x}(t^{2}-tg(t))dt.$

Then

$1^{2}g(1)=\int\limits _{1}^{1}(t^{2}-tg(t))dt=0.$

So,

$g(1)=0.$

Now use

$g(1)=\frac{1}{4}+C=0.$

Hence,

$C=-\frac{1}{4}.$

Therefore,

$g(x)=\frac{x}{4}-\frac{1}{4x^{3}}.$

Step 6: Find $g(2)$
$g(2)=\frac{2}{4}-\frac{1}{4(2^{3})}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{32}=\frac{16-1}{32}=\frac{15}{32}.$

So the correct answer is

$\dfrac{15}{32}.$

Hence, Option C.

text: The area of the region $\left \{(x,y):x^{2}-8x\leq y\leq -x\right \}$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For the region

$\{(x,y):x^{2}-8x\leq y\leq -x\},$

the lower curve is

$y=x^{2}-8x$

and the upper curve is

$y=-x.$

To find the area between the curves, we first find their points of intersection.

Set

$x^{2}-8x=-x$

$x^{2}-7x=0$

$x(x-7)=0$

So, the curves intersect at

$x=0\text{and}x=7.$

Now, on the interval $[0,7]$, the line $y=-x$ lies above the parabola $y=x^{2}-8x$.

Hence, the required area is

$\text{Area}=\int\limits _{0}^{7}\left [(-x)-(x^{2}-8x)\right ]dx.$

Simplify the integrand:

$(-x)-(x^{2}-8x)=-x-x^{2}+8x=7x-x^{2}.$

Therefore,

$\text{Area}=\int\limits _{0}^{7}(7x-x^{2})dx.$

Now integrate:

$\int (7x-x^{2})dx=\frac{7x^{2}}{2}-\frac{x^{3}}{3}.$

Applying the limits from $0$ to $7$:

$\text{Area}=\left [\frac{7x^{2}}{2}-\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right ]_{0}^{7}$

$=\left (\frac{7\cdot 49}{2}-\frac{343}{3}\right )-0$

$=\frac{343}{2}-\frac{343}{3}$

Taking LCM $6$:

$=\frac{1029-686}{6}=\frac{343}{6}.$

Hence, the correct answer is

$\dfrac{343}{6}$

So, the correct option is A.

text: The value of the integral $\int\limits _{-1}^{1}\left (\frac{x^{3}+|x|+1}{x^{2}+2|x|+1}\right )\mathrm{d}x$ is equal to:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$I=\int\limits _{-1}^{1}\left (\frac{x^{3}+|x|+1}{x^{2}+2|x|+1}\right )dx$

We will use the property of modulus carefully.

Since $|x|$ changes at $x=0$, split the integral into two parts:

$I=\int\limits _{-1}^{0}\left (\frac{x^{3}+|x|+1}{x^{2}+2|x|+1}\right )dx+\int\limits _{0}^{1}\left (\frac{x^{3}+|x|+1}{x^{2}+2|x|+1}\right )dx$

For $-1\leq x<0$
Here, $|x|=-x$.

So,

$x^{3}+|x|+1=x^{3}-x+1$

and

$x^{2}+2|x|+1=x^{2}-2x+1=(x-1)^{2}$

Thus,

$I_{1}=\int\limits _{-1}^{0}\frac{x^{3}-x+1}{(x-1)^{2}}dx$

For $0\leq x\leq 1$
Here, $|x|=x$.

So,

$x^{3}+|x|+1=x^{3}+x+1$

and

$x^{2}+2|x|+1=x^{2}+2x+1=(x+1)^{2}$

Thus,

$I_{2}=\int\limits _{0}^{1}\frac{x^{3}+x+1}{(x+1)^{2}}dx$

Hence,

$I=I_{1}+I_{2}$

Now simplify both integrands.

Simplifying $I_{1}$
We divide:

$\frac{x^{3}-x+1}{(x-1)^{2}}=\frac{x^{3}-x+1}{x^{2}-2x+1}$

On division,

$\frac{x^{3}-x+1}{x^{2}-2x+1}=x+2+\frac{2x-1}{(x-1)^{2}}$

Also,

$\frac{2x-1}{(x-1)^{2}}=\frac{2(x-1)+1}{(x-1)^{2}}=\frac{2}{x-1}+\frac{1}{(x-1)^{2}}$

So,

$I_{1}=\int\limits _{-1}^{0}\left (x+2+\frac{2}{x-1}+\frac{1}{(x-1)^{2}}\right )dx$

Integrating term by term,

$\int xdx=\frac{x^{2}}{2},\int 2dx=2x$

$\int \frac{2}{x-1}dx=2\ln |x-1|$

$\int \frac{1}{(x-1)^{2}}dx=\int (x-1)^{-2}dx=-\frac{1}{x-1}$

Therefore,

$I_{1}=\left [\frac{x^{2}}{2}+2x+2\ln |x-1|-\frac{1}{x-1}\right ]_{-1}^{0}$

At $x=0$:

$\frac{0}{2}+0+2\ln 1-\frac{1}{-1}=1$

At $x=-1$:

$\frac{1}{2}-2+2\ln 2-\frac{1}{-2}=\frac{1}{2}-2+2\ln 2+\frac{1}{2}=-1+2\ln 2$

So,

$I_{1}=1-(-1+2\ln 2)=2-2\ln 2$

Simplifying $I_{2}$
Now,

$\frac{x^{3}+x+1}{(x+1)^{2}}=\frac{x^{3}+x+1}{x^{2}+2x+1}$

On division,

$\frac{x^{3}+x+1}{(x+1)^{2}}=x-2+\frac{4x+3}{(x+1)^{2}}$

Also,

$\frac{4x+3}{(x+1)^{2}}=\frac{4(x+1)-1}{(x+1)^{2}}=\frac{4}{x+1}-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}$

So,

$I_{2}=\int\limits _{0}^{1}\left (x-2+\frac{4}{x+1}-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\right )dx$

Integrating term by term,

$I_{2}=\left [\frac{x^{2}}{2}-2x+4\ln |x+1|+\frac{1}{x+1}\right ]_{0}^{1}$

At $x=1$:

$\frac{1}{2}-2+4\ln 2+\frac{1}{2}=-1+4\ln 2$

At $x=0$:

$0-0+4\ln 1+1=1$

So,

$I_{2}=(-1+4\ln 2)-1=-2+4\ln 2$

Adding $I_{1}$ and $I_{2}$
$I=(2-2\ln 2)+(-2+4\ln 2)=2\ln 2$

Therefore,

$\int\limits _{-1}^{1}\left (\dfrac{x^{3}+|x|+1}{x^{2}+2|x|+1}\right )dx=2\log _{e}2$

So, the correct option is:

$\text{Option B}$

text: Let $\mathrm{R}=\{(x,y)\in 𝐍\times 𝐍:\log _{\mathrm{e}}(x+y)\leq 2\}$. Then the minimum number of elements, required to be added in $R$ to make it a transitive relation, is $____$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
We have  

$R=\{(x,y)\in \mathrm{ℕ}\times \mathrm{ℕ}:\ln (x+y)\leq 2\}.$

To make the relation transitive, we first find all pairs already in $R$.

Since  

$\ln (x+y)\leq 2⟺x+y\leq e^{2}.$

Now,

$e^{2}\approx 7.389.$

So, for natural numbers $x,y$, we must have

$x+y\leq 7.$

Hence,

$R=\{(x,y)\in \mathrm{ℕ}\times \mathrm{ℕ}:x+y\leq 7\}.$

Now list all such pairs:

For $x=1$: $(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(1,4),(1,5),(1,6)$

For $x=2$: $(2,1),(2,2),(2,3),(2,4),(2,5)$

For $x=3$: $(3,1),(3,2),(3,3),(3,4)$

For $x=4$: $(4,1),(4,2),(4,3)$

For $x=5$: $(5,1),(5,2)$

For $x=6$: $(6,1)$

So these are the elements of $R$.

A relation is transitive if whenever  

$(a,b)\in R\text{and}(b,c)\in R,$

then  

$(a,c)\in R.$

We need to find all pairs $(a,c)$ that must be present because of transitivity.

Step 1: Find which middle elements are possible
If $(a,b)\in R$, then

$a+b\leq 7.$

If $(b,c)\in R$, then

$b+c\leq 7.$

For a fixed $b$, this gives

$a\leq 7-b,c\leq 7-b.$

So for each $b$, transitivity demands that all pairs

$(a,c)\text{with}1\leq a\leq 7-b,1\leq c\leq 7-b$

must be in the relation.

Taking union over all possible $b\in \mathrm{ℕ}$ with at least one such pair, we get:

For $b=1$: required pairs are all

$(a,c),1\leq a\leq 6,1\leq c\leq 6.$

This is already the largest possible set forced by transitivity.

So, if relation is to be transitive, it must contain every pair

$(a,c)\in \{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\times \{1,2,3,4,5,6\}.$

That means the transitive closure must at least contain all $36$ pairs

$(a,c),1\leq a,c\leq 6.$

Step 2: Count how many of these are already in $R$
Among these $36$ pairs, $R$ already contains those with

$a+c\leq 7.$

Count them:

$a=1$: $c=1$ to $6$  $\Rightarrow 6$

$a=2$: $c=1$ to $5$  $\Rightarrow 5$

$a=3$: $c=1$ to $4$  $\Rightarrow 4$

$a=4$: $c=1$ to $3$  $\Rightarrow 3$

$a=5$: $c=1$ to $2$  $\Rightarrow 2$

$a=6$: $c=1$         $\Rightarrow 1$

Total:

$6+5+4+3+2+1=21.$

So the number of additional pairs needed is

$36-21=15.$

Step 3: Check that this is sufficient
If we add all missing pairs among

$\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\times \{1,2,3,4,5,6\},$

then the relation becomes

$\{(a,c):1\leq a\leq 6,1\leq c\leq 6\}.$

This is clearly transitive, because whenever

$(a,b)\in R\text{and}(b,c)\in R,$

all three numbers lie in $\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$, so $(a,c)$ is also in the relation.

Therefore, the minimum number of elements to be added is

$15$

text: Let the line $x-y=4$ intersect the circle $\mathrm{C}:(x-4)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}=9$ at the points Q and R . If $\mathrm{P}(α,β)$ is a point on C such that $\mathrm{PQ}=\mathrm{PR}$, then $(6α+8β)^{2}$ is equal to $____$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Since $PQ=PR$, the point $P$ must lie on the perpendicular bisector of the chord $QR$.

Now, the points $Q$ and $R$ are the intersection points of the line

$x-y=4$

with the circle

$(x-4)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}=9.$

So, $QR$ is a chord of the circle lying on the line $x-y=4$.

For a circle, the perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the centre.

The centre of the circle is

$(4,-3).$

The slope of the line $x-y=4$ is $1$, so the slope of the perpendicular bisector is $-1$.

Hence the perpendicular bisector of chord $QR$ passing through $(4,-3)$ is

$y+3=-1(x-4)$

$y+3=-x+4$

$x+y=1.$

Therefore, point $P(α,β)$ lies on both:

the circle:

$(α-4)^{2}+(β+3)^{2}=9$

the line:

$α+β=1.$

Now we need $(6α+8β)^{2}$.

Using $α+β=1$, let

$β=1-α.$

Substitute into the circle:

$(α-4)^{2}+((1-α)+3)^{2}=9$

$(α-4)^{2}+(4-α)^{2}=9$

Since $(4-α)^{2}=(α-4)^{2}$,

$2(α-4)^{2}=9$

$(α-4)^{2}=\frac{9}{2}.$

Now,

$6α+8β=6α+8(1-α)=8-2α.$

So,

$(6α+8β)^{2}=(8-2α)^{2}=4(α-4)^{2}.$

Using $(α-4)^{2}=\frac{9}{2}$,

$(6α+8β)^{2}=4\cdot \frac{9}{2}=18.$

Hence, the required value is

$18.$

text: Let the image of the point $\mathrm{P}(0,-5,0)$ in the line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y}{1}=\frac{z+1}{-2}$ be the point R and the image of the point $\mathrm{Q}\left (0,\frac{-1}{2},0\right )$ in the line $\frac{x-1}{-1}=\frac{y+9}{4}=\frac{z+1}{1}$ be the point S . Then the square of the area of the parallelogram PQRS is $____$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The first line is $(1+2t,t,-1-2t)$ with direction $(2,1,-2)$. For the foot $M$ of the perpendicular from $P(0,-5,0)$:

$2(1+2t)+(t+5)-2(-1-2t)=0\Rightarrow 9t+9=0\Rightarrow t=-1$

So $M=(-1,-1,1)$ and $R=2M-P=(-2,3,2)$.

The second line is $(1-u,-9+4u,-1+u)$ with direction $(-1,4,1)$. For the foot $N$ of the perpendicular from $Q\left (0,-\frac{1}{2},0\right )$:

$-(1-u)+4\left (4u-\frac{17}{2}\right )+(u-1)=0\Rightarrow 18u-36=0\Rightarrow u=2$

So $N=(-1,-1,1)$ and $S=2N-Q=\left (-2,-\dfrac{3}{2},2\right )$.

Now $PQ\leftarrow =\left (0,\dfrac{9}{2},0\right )=SR\leftarrow$, so $PQRS$ is a parallelogram with adjacent sides $PQ\leftarrow$ and $PS\leftarrow =\left (-2,\dfrac{7}{2},2\right )$.

$PQ\leftarrow \times PS\leftarrow =\left |\begin{array}{lll} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 0 & \frac{9}{2} & 0 \\ -2 & \frac{7}{2} & 2 \end{array}\right |=9\hat{i}+9\hat{k}$

$(\text{Area})^{2}=|PQ\leftarrow \times PS\leftarrow |^{2}=9^{2}+9^{2}=162$

Hence, the answer is 162.

text:
Let $f(x)=\left \{\begin{array}{ll} x^{3}+8; & x<0, \\ x^{2}-4; & x\geq 0, \end{array} \right.$ and $g(x)=\left \{\begin{array}{ll} (x-8)^{1/3}; & x<0, \\ (x+4)^{1/2}; & x\geq 0. \end{array} \right.$

Then the number of points, where the function $g\circ f$ is discontinuous, is $____$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
We need to find the points where the composite function $g\circ f$ is discontinuous.

That means we first find

$(g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x)).$

So we must see, for each value of $x$, which branch of $g$ will be used.

1. Given functions
$f(x)=\left \{\begin{array}{ll} x^{3}+8, & x<0, \\ x^{2}-4, & x\geq 0 \end{array} \right.$

and

$g(x)=\left \{\begin{array}{ll} (x-8)^{1/3}, & x<0, \\ (x+4)^{1/2}, & x\geq 0. \end{array} \right.$

Now,

$(g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x)).$

The definition of $g$ depends on whether its input is negative or non-negative. So we must check the sign of $f(x)$.

2. Find where $f(x)<0$ and where $f(x)\geq 0$
Case 1: $x<0$
Then

$f(x)=x^{3}+8.$

We check when this is negative:

$x^{3}+8<0⟹x^{3}<-8⟹x<-2.$

So for $x<0$:

if $x<-2$, then $f(x)<0$,

if $-2\leq x<0$, then $f(x)\geq 0$.

Case 2: $x\geq 0$
Then

$f(x)=x^{2}-4.$

We check when this is negative:

$x^{2}-4<0⟹x^{2}<4⟹-2<x<2.$

But here $x\geq 0$, so this becomes

$0\leq x<2.$

Thus for $x\geq 0$:

if $0\leq x<2$, then $f(x)<0$,

if $x\geq 2$, then $f(x)\geq 0$.

3. Write $(g\circ f)(x)$ piecewise
Now use the correct branch of $g$.

(i) When $x<-2$
Here $f(x)<0$, so use

$g(y)=(y-8)^{1/3}.$

Thus

$(g\circ f)(x)=\left ((x^{3}+8)-8\right )^{1/3}=(x^{3})^{1/3}=x.$

So for $x<-2$,

$(g\circ f)(x)=x.$

(ii) When $-2\leq x<0$
Here $f(x)\geq 0$, so use

$g(y)=\sqrt{y+4}.$

Thus

$(g\circ f)(x)=\sqrt{(x^{3}+8)+4}=\sqrt{x^{3}+12}.$

So for $-2\leq x<0$,

$(g\circ f)(x)=\sqrt{x^{3}+12}.$

(iii) When $0\leq x<2$
Here $f(x)<0$, so use

$g(y)=(y-8)^{1/3}.$

Thus

$(g\circ f)(x)=\left ((x^{2}-4)-8\right )^{1/3}=(x^{2}-12)^{1/3}.$

So for $0\leq x<2$,

$(g\circ f)(x)=(x^{2}-12)^{1/3}.$

(iv) When $x\geq 2$
Here $f(x)\geq 0$, so use

$g(y)=\sqrt{y+4}.$

Thus

$(g\circ f)(x)=\sqrt{(x^{2}-4)+4}=\sqrt{x^{2}}=x$

since $x\geq 2$.

So for $x\geq 2$,

$(g\circ f)(x)=x.$

4. Check continuity at possible boundary points
Each expression is continuous in its own interval. So we only check the joining points:

$x=-2,x=0,x=2.$

At $x=-2$
Left-hand limit:

for $x<-2$, $(g\circ f)(x)=x$, so

$\lim _{x\to -2^{-}}(g\circ f)(x)=-2.$

Right-hand limit:

for $-2\leq x<0$, $(g\circ f)(x)=\sqrt{x^{3}+12}$, so

$\lim _{x\to -2^{+}}(g\circ f)(x)=\sqrt{(-2)^{3}+12}=\sqrt{4}=2.$

Since

$-2\neq 2,$

the function is discontinuous at $x=-2$.

At $x=0$
Left-hand limit:

$\lim _{x\to 0^{-}}(g\circ f)(x)=\sqrt{0^{3}+12}=\sqrt{12}.$

Right-hand limit:

$\lim _{x\to 0^{+}}(g\circ f)(x)=(0^{2}-12)^{1/3}=(-12)^{1/3}.$

These are not equal, so discontinuous at $x=0$.

At $x=2$
Left-hand limit:

$\lim _{x\to 2^{-}}(g\circ f)(x)=(2^{2}-12)^{1/3}=(-8)^{1/3}=-2.$

Right-hand limit:

$\lim _{x\to 2^{+}}(g\circ f)(x)=2.$

These are not equal, so discontinuous at $x=2$.

5. Conclusion
The function $g\circ f$ is discontinuous at

$x=-2,x=0,x=2.$

Hence, the number of points of discontinuity is

$3.$
